newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Faro outage sends mine calculators clicking.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Faro outage sends mine calculators clicking.

text.p: Zinc and lead miners and smelters reached for their calculators on Wednesday following surprise news from Anvil Range Mining that its Faro zinc and lead mine in the Yukon will shut temporarily from December 20 because of low metal prices.

The news comes just as miners and smelters make early overtures in their so-called mating season talks to lock in treatment charges for next year's zinc and lead concentrate sales by miners to smelters.
The talks hinge on supply and demand figures over the coming year - a surplus of mined production means smelters can negotiate lower treatment charges. Less concentrates strengthens the miner's hand.
Before Anvil's announcement, the International Lead and Zinc Study Group had already forecast refined zinc demand next year would exceed production for the third year in a row.

"This is going to make people think, no question about that," a North American zinc mining official said. "This is going to be the thing that drives up zinc prices - finally a big mine has got into difficulty."
The 1996 zinc TC was pegged at $190 per tonne basis an LME price of $1,000 per tonne. Lead was settled at $175 per tonne basis LME price of $600 per tonne.
Miners said zinc prices need to be between 50 and 60 cents per pound to be competitive. LME cash zinc settled at 48 cents.
A clutch of small zinc mines have already crept on the casualty list this year, ASARCO's Leadville, Inmet Mining's Bougrine, and Denehurst's Benambra.
Noranda's Brunswick mine is expected to produce at 20 percent below capacity for most of next year, one mining source said.

An Americas mining executive noted that when Faro came back on stream some two years ago, it turned the lead concentrate market from a deficit to a surplus, enabling smelters to wrench better terms from the miners.
"The Anvil announcement will impact the lead market," the executive said.
The ILZSG had forecast that lead supply next year was due to exceed demand for the first time since 1994.

Anvil said it will continue to run its mill on previously stockpiled ore to produce concentrates at a level of about 50 percent of the intended output of 480,000 tonnes per year of zinc and lead concentrate.
The stockpile would last three to four months, Anvil said.
Faro was originally forecast to produce 140,000 tonnes of contained zinc and 100,000 tonnes of contained lead in concentrates this year.
The concentrates were marketed in Europe by Cominco Limited .
Zinc miners were already drawing comfort from two major spot deals concluded recently, by Centromin and Hindustan Zinc, both for about $160 per tonne or below once freight is deducted.
Miners were bruised by last year's big hike in zinc TCs, based on expectations of a big concentrates surplus developing near the end of 1996, but it never came.
One zinc miner said he had already offered, before Anvil's news, terms below those of 1994 when TCs were settled at $174 basis $1,000.
However, miners conceded that the concentrates market is not going to affect the zinc price significantly until the large LME stocks of metal have been reduced further.
-- Huw Jones, New York Commodities 212-859-1646
